articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designation Update
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced an Iran Designation Update on November 9, 2026. This action signifies ongoing efforts by the U.S. Treasury to target entities and individuals associated with the Iranian regime.

Further details regarding the specific individuals or entities designated, and the reasons for their inclusion, are expected to be elaborated in accompanying official statements or press releases from the Treasury Department.

This update is part of a broader strategy to exert economic pressure on Iran, which has been subject to extensive U.S. sanctions due to its nuclear program, support for terrorism, and human rights violations.

articles.headline: U.S. Imposes New Iran-Related Designations Targeting Digital Asset Sector
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026, targeting eight Canada-based money services businesses.
These businesses are accused of operating in the digital asset sector of the Iranian economy, facilitating the exchange of Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets.

Many of the designated entities have reportedly dealt with sanctioned Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset addresses linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), highlighting continued efforts to circumvent sanctions through digital means.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations; Adds Cuba Designations
body: On November 5, 2026, OFAC announced designations related to cyber-related activities and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new designations targeting Cuba.
The cyber-related designations targeted five individuals and 41 entities supporting global scam networks.

Additionally, two individuals, six entities, and two vessels were added to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List under Executive Order 14404, with the individuals listed in Cuba and Panama, and the entities in Cuba, China, and Panama.

articles.headline: U.S. Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues Venezuela General License Update
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, alongside updates to certain Iran-related listings and the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert.
The designations targeted five individuals and ten entities in India, Singapore, and Turkey, under E.O. 13902 or the Iran-related conventional-arms sanctions authority.

OFAC also issued Venezuela General License 5AA, replacing General License 5Z and postponing until December 18, 2026, the authorization for specified transactions involving the PDVSA 2020 8.5 percent bond.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment signifies a modification to existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.
General Licenses typically permit specific activities that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs, and amendments can broaden or narrow the scope of such permitted activities.
The details of this amended license would specify the types of transactions or activities that are now authorized or subject to new conditions, impacting various sectors dealing with Iran.

The specific details of the designated entities and the nature of their involvement in activities warranting sanctions are typically outlined in accompanying press releases from the Treasury Department.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related and Russia-Related General Licenses, Amends FAQs
body: On October 21, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses, along with amendments to Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs).
These General Licenses provide authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the respective sanctions programs, potentially easing restrictions in specific areas.
The amendments to the FAQs aim to provide clarity and guidance to the public regarding compliance with OFAC regulations concerning Iran and Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes PAIPA Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: On October 19, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA), along with the issuance of associated General Licenses.

These designations targeted five Chinese entities over alleged theft of trade secrets related to Google's AI technology, marking the second-ever use of PAIPA and its first application against Chinese entities.
The associated General Licenses aim to mitigate unintended consequences of the sanctions, allowing for certain transactions or activities that would otherwise be prohibited.

articles.headline: UN Watchdog Urges Iran to Reopen Nuclear Facilities for Inspection
body: The UN nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), has called on Iran to urgently allow inspections at its nuclear facilities, expressing increasing concern over Iran's refusal to grant access to an underground uranium enrichment facility in Isfahan.
Highly enriched uranium is believed to be buried at the Isfahan site, which the IAEA has never been able to inspect.
This call comes amid heightened tensions and ongoing international efforts to monitor Iran's nuclear program.

articles.headline: U.S. Denies Iranian Claim of Radar Strike in Bahrain, Confirms Drone Interception
body: The U.S. military on Friday denied claims by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that it had destroyed a U.S. early-warning radar installation in Bahrain.
U.S. Central Command acknowledged that Iran had launched two attack drones at Bahrain but stated that both were shot down by U.S. forces, causing no injuries or damage.
Iranian state media had published reports and an image allegedly showing the damaged radar station, a claim refuted by the U.S. military.

articles.headline: Iran Links Strait of Hormuz Reopening to U.S. Meeting Demands
body: Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, stated on November 11, 2026, that Iran will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States fulfills Tehran's seven conditions for peace talks.
These conditions reportedly include the lifting of U.S. sanctions and the naval blockade, an end to hostilities on all fronts, and the withdrawal of U.S. forces.
Rezaei emphasized that Tehran expects a clear and official response from Washington, describing previous U.S. responses as insufficient and misleading.

articles.headline: BIS Extends Suspension of 'Affiliates Rule' for Entity List Enforcement
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has further extended the suspension of its interim final rule, known as the 'Affiliates Rule,' until January 10, 2027.

This rule, if implemented, would apply export control restrictions to any entity that is 50% or more owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more entities on the BIS Entity List or Military End-User List.
The extension, published in the Federal Register, provides affected companies with additional time to prepare for the expanded customer due diligence burdens that the rule would entail.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
